To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the reflectivity of mirrors acted on by a laser beam does not change until the moment when intense evaporation of metal occurs.
the reflection coefficient of a metal mirror acted on by laser pulses is not affected by the energy density of the radiation until the energy density reaches the evaporation energy density.

the reflectivity of the metals investigated remained constant right up till the energy density at the metal surface at which intense evaption of the metal occurred, but there was a substantial reduction when an absorbing discharge occurred in the vapor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effect of the intensity of laser radiation on the reflectivity of the surface of metals.
the measurement of the reflection coefficient of metal mirrors acted upon by laser radiation.
the study of the reflectivity and the heating of metal mirrors by intense pulsed radiation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the reflection coefficient of a mirror remains constant up to an energy density of 0.5 J/cm2.
the reflection coefficients of copper, aluminum and stainless steel mirrors are constant right up to an energy density of ~0.5–1 J/cm ^{2}.
the reflectivity of the mirrors was constant up to a critical energy density at which the metal evaporated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it is possible to use metal mirrors for focusing laser radiation of the required energy density, provided that they are not heated up to the point of evaporation.

it is not possible to use the linear theory to describe the heating of metal surfaces acted on by laser pulses of 400 nsec duration, and that a substantial reduction in reflection coefficient of metal mirrors can occur at an energy density at which no visible changes in the surface are observed.

the reflection coefficient of a mirror acted on by a laser pulse of ~70 J energy and ~400 nsec length is practically unchanged until the energy density at the surface reaches 10 9 J/m 2, at which time intense evaporation of metal begins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for the conditions of our experiment, there is a substantial increase in the reflection coefficient of a metal mirror when the temperature of its surface exceeds the boiling point of the metal.
it is possible to use metal mirrors as reflectors of powerful laser pulses, even when the energy density of the radiation is high enough for the formation of a discharge in the vapor of the metal.
the reflectivity of a metal mirror is not affected by laser irradiation up to the energy at which intense evapora-tion of the metal occurs.
